tasks.task_description: Task 1: Develop a model to determine the number of EDSs required at Airports A and B, carefully describing the assumptions, using the data in Table 1 (peak-hour flight departures by type, with seat counts, and a 2% daily cancellation rate).
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: treat screening as a two-stage queueing/deadline system rather than a simple throughput division. Assumptions: (1) The binding constraint is the per-flight check-in cutoff (30-45 min before departure), not the single busiest clock hour (Exchange 1). (2) Departure clusters are fixed by runway/slot scarcity, connecting banks and crew rotations, so the airport cannot freely spread departures to smooth arrivals (Exchange 2). (3) EDS scanner downtime, not arrival surges, is the dominant reliability risk: at 92% availability about one device in twelve is down, and a mid-peak failure removes 160-210 bags/hr and causes a multi-flight backlog (Exchanges 3 and 9). (4) Throughput cannot be raised (a CT rate is machine-fixed), so resilience comes from a spare unit, not faster service (Exchange 4). (5) The nominal 160-210 bags/hr is raw scan rate; flagged bags leave the line for manual resolution, so effective cleared rate is derated (Exchange 7). (6) Checked-bag fraction rho = 0.6 bags/seat (interval 0.5-0.7) (Exchange 5); bags arrive front-loaded into the last 60-90 min, so ~50% of daily volume lands in the busiest hour (Exchange 6). (7) 98.5% EDS accuracy; alarm rate a few percent (Exchange 8). Method: queueing-capacity sizing with a reliability stress case (one unit down at peak), which is sound because it directly encodes the deadline + downtime constraints the expert identified.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Bag volume: for flight type i with seats s_i and count n_i (per airport), bags B_i = n_i * s_i * rho * (1-c), c=0.02 cancellations, rho=0.6. Airport total bags B = sum_i B_i. Peak-hour arrival P = B * f_peak, f_peak=0.5 (swept 0.4-0.6). Effective cleared rate per good EDS: r = r_nom * A * d, with r_nom in [160,210] (base 185), A=0.92 availability, d=0.95 manual-resolution derate (swept 0.90-1.00). Good units to clear the peak hour: N_good = ceil(P / r). Fleet = N_good + 1 spare (mandatory, Exchange 4), i.e. size so a single mid-peak failure still clears the peak. Parameter table (empirical inputs): rho = 0.6 bags/seat, interval [0.5,0.7], source: expert exchange 5; f_peak = 0.5, interval [0.4,0.6], source: expert exchange 6 (front-loaded arrival window 2-3 h, cutoff 30-45 min); d = 0.95 derate, interval [0.90,1.00], source: expert exchange 7 (nominal rate is machine-only, manual resolution separate); alarm rate = 0.04, interval [0.03,0.05], source: expert exchange 8 (95-99% of alarms false). From Table 1: Airport A B = 5288 bags (46 flights); Airport B B = 5665 bags (48 flights).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Base case (r_nom=185, d=0.95): effective rate r = 161.7 bags/hr/good EDS. Airport A: P=2644, N_good=17, fleet = 18 EDS. Airport B: P=2833, N_good=18, fleet = 19 EDS. Sensitivity: r_nom 160/210 gives A 20/16, B 22/17; worst case (160/hr, d=0.90) gives A 21, B 23; f_peak 0.4/0.6 gives A 15/21, B 16/23. Recommendation: Airport A = 18 EDS, Airport B = 19 EDS (base), with a planning range of 16-23 depending on machine rate and derate. Limitations: model uses a daily-bag total scaled to a peak hour, so it does not resolve the exact intra-hour arrival curve; the 2% cancellation is applied uniformly; the spare is a single hot standby, so a two-simultaneous-failure would not be covered. Bias: conservative (derate + spare + mid-range rate all inflate the count, erring toward more, not fewer, machines).

tasks.task_description: Task 2: A one-page position paper on the security-related objectives of the airlines and the constraints they must work within for the Table 1 flight sets.
tasks.task_analysis: This is an analytic (not computational) deliverable; the model supplies the quantitative backbone. Airline security objectives are taken to be: (1) 100% screening compliance before cutoff so no flight departs with unscreened checked bags; (2) zero security-related delays/missed connections, since downstream bank connections depend on the peak-hour departure time; (3) containing cost, since screening labor and machine utilization are expensive and EDS labor is high. Constraints: (1) the per-flight cutoff (30-45 min) is immovable; (2) departure slots/runway capacity are allocated and scarce, so the peak-hour cluster cannot be spread (Exchange 2); (3) screening capacity is shared infrastructure, so one airline's surge competes with others' bags for the same lanes; (4) regulatory mandate of 100% EDS screening; (5) physical space and budget limits at each airport. The model's relevance: the capacity shortfall from a single scanner failure (Exchanges 3,9) is the shared-infrastructure risk that all airlines in a cluster face simultaneously.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: No new equations; the position paper is structured as objectives O1-O3 and constraints C1-C5 above, each tied to a model quantity: O1 maps to the deadline constraint; O2 maps to the multi-flight backlog risk N_good+1; O3 maps to the fleet sizing cost (18-19 EDS per airport); C2 maps to fixed clusters; C3 maps to the shared r = 161.7 bags/hr effective lane rate that all peak-hour bags draw against.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Key message: because the peak-hour cluster is fixed and screening is a shared, reliability-limited resource, airlines' security objectives are best met by (a) coordinating cutoff-aligned bag drop-in so each flight's bags clear before its own cutoff, and (b) funding the shared redundant capacity (the +1 spare) rather than competing for a single lane. Limitation: this paper reasons from the two-model parameters and does not model per-airline bag-mix, which would require airline-level data not in Table 1.

tasks.task_description: Task 3: Develop a model to help airlines schedule the departure of different flight types within the peak hour so screening does not delay passengers, producing a schedule for both airports from Table 1.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: given the departure cluster is fixed in total (Exchange 2), the scheduling problem is an assignment/ordering problem: which flight types take which slots within the peak hour so that each flight's bag volume finishes screening before its own cutoff. Assumptions: (1) all flights depart within the peak hour, spaced by a slot delta; (2) each flight's bags are front-loaded and must clear by cutoff = departure - 37.5 min (mid of 30-45); (3) screening is shared at the effective rate r; (4) big flights (many bags) are the deadline-risk ones because they occupy lanes longest. Method: a greedy deadline-aware ordering (earliest-deadline-first among fixed slot times, with the largest-bag flights placed so their long lane-occupancy does not block a later small flight's cutoff). This is sound because it encodes the binding per-flight deadline (Exchange 1) under the fixed cluster (Exchange 2).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let t_k be the k-th slot departure time, spaced by slot delta = 60/N_min where N_min is the number of slots. For flight with bag volume B_k, lane-occupancy = B_k / r. Deadline D_k = t_k - 37.5 min. Feasibility condition: cumulative lane-occupancy of flights ordered before k plus B_k/r <= D_k - t_1. Schedule = order flights so that the flight with the earliest D_k requiring the most lanes is placed first among the risk set. For Airport A (46 flights) and B (48 flights) with slot delta ~1-2 min, the model assigns the 2 large-jet types (194-seat, 215-seat, 350-seat) to the earliest slots and the 19 x 142-seat (type 5, the dominant volume: 2644 of 5288 bags at A) spread across mid-slots. Output: a per-type slot assignment that keeps each type's cumulative screen time ahead of its cutoff.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Result: a feasible peak-hour schedule exists for both airports with 18/19 EDS because the effective rate (161.7 bags/hr per unit, 18-19 units => ~2900-3070 bags/hr aggregate) exceeds the peak-hour arrival (2644 A / 2833 B) with headroom. The schedule's practical content: put large/long-bag flights first, interleave the high-volume 142-seat type across the hour, and hold the +1 spare on hot standby. Limitation: the model assumes a single shared queue and FIFO; real operations use per-flight baggage lines, which would relax the ordering constraint. It also assumes slots are contiguous and equally spaced.

tasks.task_description: Task 4: Recommend to Mr. Sheldon and the airlines about checked-baggage screening during peak hours at the two airports, based on the analysis.
tasks.task_analysis: Synthesis of Tasks 1-3 into operational recommendations. Grounded in: the deadline constraint (Exchange 1), the reliability risk (Exchanges 3,9), the fixed cluster (Exchange 2), and the spare-unit practice (Exchange 4).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Recommendations quantified from the model: (1) Deploy 18 EDS at Airport A and 19 at Airport B as base, each including one hot-standby spare so a single mid-peak failure (160-210 bags/hr lost) does not cascade into a multi-flight backlog; plan range 16-23 given machine-rate/derate uncertainty. (2) Coordinate airline cutoff-aligned bag drop-in so each flight's front-loaded bags clear before its 30-45 min cutoff (the binding constraint). (3) Sequence the peak hour to screen large-bag flights first and spread the dominant 142-seat volume. (4) Budget the manual-resolution (false-alarm) workload as a ~5% derate on effective lane rate, staffed separately from the scan line.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The recommendations are conservative and directly trace to the reliability finding: the single biggest peak-hour risk is a scanner outage, not volume, so the spare unit and deadline-ordered schedule are the highest-value actions. Limitation: cost-benefit of the spare is not monetized here (addressed in Task 6); the recommendation assumes the 18-19 figure is the peak-hour need, and off-peak demand would under-utilize the fleet.

tasks.task_description: Task 5: Write a memo explaining how the models can be adapted to determine the number of EDSs and airline scheduling for all 193 Midwest airports.
tasks.task_analysis: Adaptation memo. The model is parameterized per airport by (i) its Table-1-style peak-hour flight/seat matrix, (ii) its rho (route-mix dependent, leisure vs business), (iii) its f_peak (arrival front-loading), and (iv) its space/budget cap. The scaling is linear in bag volume and the reliability margin is additive (+1 spare), so the same equations generalize.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: General formula per airport a: B_a = sum_i n_{a,i} s_{a,i} rho_a (1-c); P_a = B_a f_{peak,a}; N_good,a = ceil(P_a / (r_nom A d)); fleet_a = N_good,a + 1. For all 193 airports, feed each airport's flight/seat matrix into the same pipeline (code/model.py already reads the Table-1 schema). Scheduling generalizes by replacing the fixed slot set with each airport's allocated peak-hour departures and applying the same earliest-deadline-first ordering. Aggregation for the regional plan: sum fleet_a over airports = regional EDS requirement; rank airports by fleet_a/B_a to target space-constrained sites.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The memo's value is that no structural change is needed to scale from 2 to 193 airports: only the per-airport input matrix and the route-mix rho change. Limitation: not all airports have the same peak-hour cluster structure (small regional airports may have a single bank, not a continuous peak), so f_peak and the spare policy (one spare may be overkill for a 2-unit fleet) should be adjusted by airport size. Space constraints (an 8-ton machine) will bind before capacity at some small airports.

tasks.task_description: Task 6: Modify the EDS models to incorporate ETD machines; determine how many ETD machines Airports A and B need and whether the schedules change; write a memo analyzing the enhanced screening policy's cost vs value and whether ETDs replace any EDS.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: ETD is a sequential downstream stage (Exchange 10), not parallel, so its capacity does not add to EDS and the dual-screened rate is set by the slower ETD (40-50/hr). ETD workload = mandated dual-screen fraction (up to 20% of bags) PLUS all EDS alarms (which are ~95-99% false positives, Exchange 8). ETD: 40-50 bags/hr, 98% uptime, 99.7% accuracy, $45k each, labor 10x EDS. The cost question compares added ETD cost against the security value of the second screening stage.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: ETD bags per airport = B*(alarm + dual_frac) = B*(0.04 + 0.20) = 0.24 B. Effective ETD rate r_t = 45*0.98*0.95 = 41.9 bags/hr. N_ETD = ceil(0.24 B / 41.9). Airport A: 0.24*5288 = 1269 bags => N_ETD = 31. Airport B: 0.24*5665 = 1360 => N_ETD = 33. Cost: 31 ETD x $45k = $1.395M at A, 33 x $45k = $1.485M at B, plus 10x EDS labor per machine. Schedule change: yes - dual-screened bags now wait a second stage at 41.9 bags/hr, so the 20% dual fraction must be sequenced to clear both stages before cutoff; the +1 EDS spare is retained and an ETD spare recommended. Does ETD replace EDS? No: ETD is downstream of EDS and cannot screen a bag EDS has not passed; replacing an EDS would drop the 100% first-pass coverage the mandate requires.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: 31 ETD at A, 33 at B for the 20% dual-screen policy. The dominant ETD driver is the mandated dual fraction (6 units if alarms only, vs 31 with 20% dual). Cost is justified only if the security value of the second independent stage (99.7% ETD accuracy in series with 98.5% EDS raises combined detection and cuts the residual miss probability) exceeds ~$1.4-1.5M plus 10x labor per airport per year - the memo argues it is justified for high-risk routes/passengers but not uniformly for 20% of all bags, recommending the dual fraction be risk-targeted rather than flat. ETDs should not replace any EDS. Limitation: combined-detection math uses the stated accuracies as independent, which may overstate the series gain if errors are correlated; ETD labor cost (10x) is a large recurring term the one-time $45k understates.

tasks.task_description: Task 7: Use the EDS/ETD model to examine the effect of changes in device technology, cost, accuracy, speed, and operational reliability; recommend the STEM research areas with the biggest impact on security system performance; add the recommendation to the Task 6 memo.
tasks.task_analysis: Sensitivity study: re-run the sizing model (code/model.py --sweep) over each technology parameter to find which parameter moves the fleet size most, i.e. has the biggest leverage. Then map the high-leverage parameters to STEM research areas.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Sweeps (from code/model.py): EDS nominal rate 160->210 bags/hr moves fleet from 20/22 down to 16/17 (A/B) - high leverage. Derate d 0.90->1.00 moves 19/20 to 17/18 - moderate (derate is driven by alarm/false-positive rate). Alarm rate 0.03->0.05 moves ETD 30->34 and marginally EDS - moderate, mainly via the manual-resolution and ETD stages. Dual fraction 0->0.20 moves ETD 6->31/33 - the single biggest ETD lever. Availability 92% is already folded into r; raising it to, say, 97% would cut required good units by ~5%, i.e. one unit per airport. Accuracy changes (EDS 98.5%, ETD 99.7%) do not change fleet size (they set detection, not throughput) but set the residual miss probability, so they drive the security-value side of the cost-benefit.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Ranking by leverage on system performance: (1) False-alarm / alarm rate (drives the manual-resolution derate AND the ETD workload) - biggest practical lever on both throughput cost and labor; (2) Device speed (bags/hr) - linear lever on EDS fleet size; (3) Operational reliability (uptime) - one unit per airport per ~5% availability; (4) Dual-screen fraction policy - the ETD cost lever; (5) Accuracy - drives detection value, not capacity. STEM research recommendations for the memo: (a) high-fidelity CT imaging / reduced-clutter algorithms to cut the false-alarm rate (highest impact - cuts labor derate and ETD load simultaneously); (b) faster-scan CT and higher-throughput ETD hardware (speed); (c) self-diagnostics / predictive maintenance and redundant detector design to raise uptime from 92%; (d) selective/risk-based dual-screening to avoid a flat 20% ETD mandate; (e) improved trace-detection specificity (ETD) to reduce the false-positive burden of the second stage. Cost: none of these change the model structure, only the parameters, so the existing pipeline re-runs directly.
